report.source_text:
Frontal and frog-leg radiographs (Figure 1A, 1B) of the pelvis were ordered for assessment.
Radiographs revealed components of a healing right-sided ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture and a 5.8cm cluster of well-corticated, ovoid and crescent-shaped calcifications in the soft tissues near the ischial tuberosity and adjacent to the avulsed bone fragment. The affected ischial tuberosity displayed lucency and irregular margins.

report.source_text: The patient was expected to make a full recovery with conservative management including rest, physical therapy, and progressive return to activity. The patient’s right ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture improved clinically over several months and he was able to make a gradual return to his usual activities and sports.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history presented to orthopedics with a 2-month history of right hip pain following a fall during football, during which he heard a popping sound. He reported localized pain at the right ischial tuberosity with posterior leg tingling to mid-thigh and exacerbation with activity. Physical examination revealed decreased strength (3/5) with resisted knee flexion. Plain radiographs (frontal and frog-leg views) confirmed a healing right ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture with a 5.8 cm cluster of well-corticated calcifications in adjacent soft tissues and lucency with irregular margins at the ischial tuberosity. MRI confirmed the calcifications with dark signal on T1 and T2 weighted images. The patient was managed conservatively with rest, physical therapy, and progressive return to activity, achieving full recovery and gradual return to sports over several months.
